title: Dunes
subtitle: A last wagon train, a stranded steamer, and a town with water until December.
story:
It is October 1928, and the diamond town's tanks run dry on 17 December. The company has written the town off. Its last water steamer, with a sea-water condenser aboard, lies stranded up the coast beyond a breach the storm cut through the sand spit, and the wagon trains are leaving across the desert. You stayed, with a few oxen left for one last train.

The company left its wagon ledger behind: how many days each past train took to cross, and this season's trains. Use it to work out what sets a crossing time, and whether the last train, carrying everyone who remains, can cross within the company's 14-day limit. The town has given up on the steamer too: it says the bar at the breach never comes dry before the water runs out. Go down the cliff behind the general store, cross the dunes to the flats, and test that on the engineer's tide machine in his wrecked hut above the ford. Then work out when to set off to haul the condenser home.
escapeBrief: To get out you worked out when to set off to haul the condenser back from the stranded water steamer. It is 1928; the river has not flooded in two years, the company has abandoned the town and stopped the water shipments, and its last steamer, carrying a sea-water condenser, lies beyond a breach the storm cut through the sand spit. The town's tanks last 70 days, to 17 December. The town has given up: it holds two of the engineer's four pulleys, the moon's and the sun's, and on its two-peg bench machine the water over the bar never drops below the wading line before the tanks run dry, so most people are leaving by land. You took those two pulleys down with you, found the other two in the dunes and on the flats, and rebuilt the engineer's full tide machine in his wrecked hut. A bigger pulley swings the wire further, so which pulley goes on which shaft says how much each rhythm moves the water, and the datum screw sets the average water level; the storm had knocked it out of true. Setting the datum on one of the engineer's measured depths and cranking to the others showed which way round the last two pulleys go: only the right order puts the pen on all three. A survey stake on the flats gave the bar's length, 1,200 m, and the haul gang's note in the store gave the sledge's pace, 400 m a day, so the bar had to stay dry for three days. Cranking forward, it does that only once before the water runs out, from the evening of 7 December, so you set off on 7, 8 or 9 December and rallied the town. The town's machine left two rhythms out, and the machine as found sat on the wrong average level. Adding the missing inputs, each weighted by how much it matters, fitting the average level as well, checking the result against what was measured, and beating the simpler model everyone trusted is exactly what a multiple regression does, on the machine or in R.

done.title: The last train stays
done.body: The wagons line said a small train would cross comfortably inside the limit. The whole ledger says otherwise: the load on each ox sets the crossing time, and the number of wagons barely matters. The last train, with so few oxen pulling so much, would still be out in the desert long after the limit. Nobody leaves by land now. Everything rests on the steamer and the bar at the breach.

escapeDone.title: The bar comes dry
escapeDone.body: On the morning you chose, the water drains off the bar and the town's carts roll out behind you across the wet sand. In the steamer's hold the condenser sits where the storm left it, whole. There are days of hauling ahead, and the tide will hold off just long enough. The town will have water again.

On the cliff top a half-abandoned diamond town of grand gabled houses in faded pastel plaster with corrugated-iron roofs, sand drifting into their doorways, a timber winch frame on the cliff lip; to its right a stone flight of canal locks climbs from a walled harbour basin behind a rubble breakwater. plannedHotspots.body: These are Cape fur seals. Their breeding season begins in the middle of October, when the bulls haul out onto the rocks to fight for territory. hotspots.label: The fur seals
hotspots.title: Seals and the strandwolf
hotspots.body: These are Cape fur seals. Their breeding season begins in the middle of October, when the bulls haul out onto the rocks to fight for territory. On this coast the pups are hunted from the land by black-backed jackals and by the brown hyena, which people here call the strandwolf, the beach wolf. In the Namib the strandwolf lives near seal colonies like this one, and even in abandoned diamond-mining towns.
hotspots.credit: Sources: Wikipedia, Cape fur seal and Brown hyena.

plannedHotspots.title: The ship the desert swallowed
plannedHotspots.body: Ships really were swallowed by this coast. The Eduard Bohlen ran aground in thick fog while landing equipment for a diamond mine, and the shore has since built out around her, so her wreck now lies in the sand, far from the water. Miners later used her as a hotel. The whole coast is named for the whale and seal bones that once littered it, and its heavy surf let boats come ashore but made it hard to launch them again.
plannedHotspots.credit: Sources: Wikipedia, Eduard Bohlen and Skeleton Coast.

ladderPlain.text: In the first puzzle you fit a straight line of crossing time against the number of wagons in each train and read its slope: each extra wagon went with about 0.39 more days on the crossing.
In the second puzzle you used that wagons line to predict the crossing time of a train that had just left, the Desert_Rose, and it came out at about 13.2 days, inside the 14-day limit.
In the third puzzle you scaled all six measurements, fit them together and compared their coefficients: the load on each ox had by far the largest effect, and the number of wagons came last.
In the final puzzle you predicted your own last train's crossing from all six measurements and got about 17.8 days, over the 14-day limit, while the wagons line alone said about 8.9 days.

To get out you set the tide machine's starting level from the engineer's logbook, mounted all four pulleys so the pen added up their rhythms, and found the only three dry days long enough for the haul before the water ran out, 7, 8 or 9 December.
